timelineEvents.title: Mediterranean seafaring networks
timelineEvents.summary: Traditional reconstructions connect western, Aegean and Anatolian seafarers through exchange, service and raids; their homelands remain disputed.
timelineEvents.details: This opening context introduces the selected reconstruction, not a new event dated precisely to 1300 BCE. Sardinian pottery at Hala Sultan Tekke supports long-distance Mediterranean contacts; it does not identify every traveller as Sherden or prove one ethnic migration route. Egyptian evidence records service and raids in later episodes. Western-to-eastern and eastern-origin models remain alternatives. No population or additional journey is inferred from these objects.
timelineEvents.label: Mediterranean · seafaring networks

timelineEvents.title: Sherden raid, capture and Egyptian service
timelineEvents.summary: Egypt defeats a Sherden seaborne raid. Captured warriors subsequently enter Egyptian service; the group is not annihilated.
timelineEvents.details: The Tanis rhetorical stela and Aswan year 2 text provide the early Ramesside context. The displayed date and Nile Delta coordinate are approximate regional reconstructions, not a located landing or an exact casualty count. Sherden captured here and Sherden in later hostile forces must not be treated as one undifferentiated army.

sources.title: Abbas 2017, A Survey of the Military Role of the Sherden Warriors, ENiM 10, pp. 7–23

timelineEvents.label: Egypt · Sherden raid

timelineEvents.title: Sherden in Egypt’s forces at Kadesh
timelineEvents.summary: Sherden fight in Egyptian service at Kadesh. A shared group name does not mean every later Sherden community is an enemy.
timelineEvents.details: Egyptian narratives and reliefs place captured Sherden in Ramesses II’s forces, including the royal guard. Lukka are named among Hittite allies in the Kadesh campaign. These are different military affiliations. The solar date is conventional, and a group-level continuity link does not prove that later records name the same individuals.

timelineEvents.title: Perire: Merneptah defeats a Libyan-led coalition
timelineEvents.summary: A Libyan-led coalition is defeated in the western Delta. Egyptian records distinguish enemy dead, living captives and the fleeing Libyan ruler.
timelineEvents.details: Karnak names Meryey’s Libyan forces with Ekwesh, Teresh, Lukka, Sherden and Shekelesh. Its damaged account lists slain enemies and living prisoners separately. Hands and genital trophies are counting units for the dead, not extra people to add to the associated totals; the text specifically associates Ekwesh hand-taking with absence of foreskins. Athribis and Karnak preserve different or damaged figures. Familiar Medinet Habu piles of hands and phalli belong to Ramesses III’s year 5 Libyan victory, a later event. Perire’s coordinate is a western-Delta proxy. The existing 1,000/3,000/4,000 modeled deaths are separate visualization scenarios, not exact reconstructed source totals. Meryey’s flight supports rout; it does not document the destination of every allied survivor.

sources.title: Manassa 2003, The Great Karnak Inscription of Merneptah, Yale Egyptological Studies 5
Emanuel 2018, Black Ships and Sea Raiders, pp. 73–77,155–157
Edgerton and Wilson 1936, Historical Records of Ramses III: The Texts in Medinet Habu Volumes I and II, SAOC 12

timelineEvents.title: Hattusa: abandonment and burning
timelineEvents.dateLabel: Around 1200–1190 BCE; individual fires not securely synchronized
timelineEvents.summary: The Hittite capital is largely abandoned; several monumental buildings burn. Attackers are unknown.
timelineEvents.details: Official buildings were cleared of portable contents, and the site lacks a uniform destruction layer demonstrating a single assault. Some fires may follow abandonment and are not securely dated together. The imperial collapse and burnt buildings are not proof that a Sea Peoples army marched inland and sacked Hattusa. Later limited occupation continued. This event therefore marks capital abandonment and burning, without inventing an attacker or invasion route.
timelineEvents.label: Hattusa · abandonment and fire

timelineEvents.title: Midea: fire and structural collapse
timelineEvents.summary: Midea is destroyed and rebuilt on a smaller scale. The cause is disputed.
timelineEvents.details: Excavation records burnt deposits, collapsed masonry and human remains. Earthquake and hostile-attack explanations have both been proposed; the HERACLES study challenged the earthquake hypothesis. The physical destruction is firmer than any claim about the attackers, whose identity remains unknown.
timelineEvents.label: Midea · destruction

timelineEvents.title: Mycenae: palatial destruction
timelineEvents.dateLabel: Around 1200–1190 BCE · end of LH IIIB
timelineEvents.summary: Mycenae’s palace system ends amid destruction. The attackers, if any, are unidentified.
timelineEvents.details: Several destruction episodes affected Mycenae, including earlier damage to buildings outside the citadel. The final palatial horizon belongs near the LH IIIB–IIIC transition. These episodes should not be combined into a single dated Sea Peoples conquest; neither the destruction deposits nor the later traditions identify a particular invading people.
timelineEvents.label: Mycenae · destruction

timelineEvents.title: Pylos: the palace burns
timelineEvents.dateLabel: Late 13th / early 12th century BCE · often c.1180
timelineEvents.summary: A major fire destroys the Palace of Nestor and preserves its Linear B archive.
timelineEvents.details: The excavators’ Cincinnati account places the final fire around 1180 BCE; the Greek Ephorate uses the broader late-13th/early-12th-century period. The administrative palace was not rebuilt. Its military preparations and destruction can support a warfare interpretation, but do not name the attackers or prove a Sea Peoples assault.

timelineEvents.title: Tiryns: destruction and rebuilding
timelineEvents.summary: The palace and Lower Citadel suffer destruction; the settlement rebuilds and expands.
timelineEvents.details: The DAI excavation team documents the palatial destruction and substantial post-palatial rebuilding. A later archaeoseismic reassessment found the traditional earthquake explanation unconvincing. That finding does not identify an invading army. Warfare or deliberate burning remain interpretations; a specific Sea Peoples attribution is unproven.
timelineEvents.label: Tiryns · destruction

timelineEvents.title: Tarsus: an uneven Bronze–Iron transition
timelineEvents.dateLabel: Early 12th century BCE · chronology and interpretation debated
timelineEvents.summary: Cilicia’s settlement and pottery traditions change unevenly; a universal Sea Peoples sack is unproven.
timelineEvents.details: Tarsus has multiple Late Bronze phases, including a substantial earlier conflagration, followed by a complex transition and local painted pottery. These should not be flattened into one securely dated 1200 BCE attack. Aegean-style vessels can reflect imports, local production and interaction as well as mobility; they do not identify a conquering ethnic army.
timelineEvents.label: Tarsus · regional transition

timelineEvents.title: Carchemish: continuity after imperial collapse
timelineEvents.dateLabel: 12th century BCE · continued urban and political life
timelineEvents.summary: Carchemish continues as a Hittite successor centre rather than sharing one universal destruction.
timelineEvents.details: The Turco-Italian excavators document substantial continuity into Iron I. One Late Bronze administrative complex was levelled and sealed without evidence of fire or violent destruction, while the public urban core persisted. Egyptian royal claims that include Carchemish among defeated lands are not a literal site-by-site destruction inventory.
timelineEvents.label: Carchemish · continuity

timelineEvents.title: Cilicia: Aegean connections and local continuity
timelineEvents.dateLabel: Early 12th century BCE · broad archaeological period
timelineEvents.summary: Aegean-style pottery and continuing local traditions mark changing Cilician communities.
timelineEvents.details: The regional sequence varies between sites. Imports, local imitation, trade and population movement are competing or complementary explanations. Later Danuna/Hiyawa identifications do not turn every 12th-century deposit into an exact ethnic migration or a Sea Peoples conquest. The caption supplies regional context, not an added population estimate.

timelineEvents.title: Ugarit: destruction of the port kingdom
timelineEvents.summary: Ugarit is destroyed. Letters also report enemy ships burning settlements in its territory.
timelineEvents.details: The French excavators date the final destruction broadly around 1190/1180 BCE. Ammurapi’s correspondence describes hostile ships and damage to towns, but does not name the enemy people. Those raids need not be the same episode as the capital’s final fall. A Sea Peoples connection is a reconstruction, not a securely named attacker or a documented exact sailing route.
timelineEvents.label: Ugarit · destruction

timelineEvents.title: Troy VIIa: destruction and rebuilding
timelineEvents.dateLabel: Around 1190–1180 BCE · end of Troy VIIa
timelineEvents.summary: Troy VIIa ends in destruction and is followed by renewed settlement.
timelineEvents.details: Excavation and ceramic chronology distinguish this horizon from the earlier end of Troy VI. Blegen linked VIIa’s destruction with warfare and the later Trojan War tradition, but that interpretation does not identify Sea Peoples attackers. The historical circumstances and any connection with epic remain debated.

timelineEvents.title: Dor: continuity and maritime interaction
timelineEvents.summary: Dor’s coastal society combines local continuity with Cypriot and other maritime contacts.
timelineEvents.details: The final excavation reports document gradual architectural and ceramic development rather than a demonstrated replacement by one invading people. A later literary association with Tjeker/Sikil does not date an exact 1175 BCE arrival. External-arrival and local-integration reconstructions remain alternatives; this model window changes with the selected chronology without changing the evidence.

timelineEvents.title: Ramesses III’s naval battle at the river mouths
timelineEvents.summary: Year8 records both land and naval fighting. Some enemies die, while captives survive; the surviving Egypt-bound dots continue into residence.
timelineEvents.details: Ramesses III records land fighting and a naval battle at the river mouths in his year 8. The usual c. 1177/1175 BCE date depends on Egyptian chronology; this map uses 1175. The exact battlefield locations, relationship and sequence of the scenes are debated. Both events share one display year; authored list order does not establish a historical sequence. The river-mouth coordinate is an eastern-Delta display proxy; ancient channels and the exact engagement site are uncertain. Royal claims of utter destruction cannot be read as the death of every member of every named people. Papyrus Harris I also records captured Sherden and Weshesh brought to Egypt and settled in strongholds. The model’s Egyptian settler envelope represents surviving captive/resident households, not the gross hostile army; it supplies no numeric year 8 death count or invented killed-to-captive ratio.

timelineEvents.title: Kilise Tepe: destruction during the transition
timelineEvents.dateLabel: 12th century BCE · after the Phase IId LH IIIC floor
timelineEvents.summary: Successive phases of the Stele Building burn; this is not one proven 1200 BCE invasion.
timelineEvents.details: The excavators distinguish fires ending Phases IIc and IId and a separate abandonment in the Central Strip. Mycenaean-type pottery on IId floors places the later fire after occupation in the first half of the 12th century. Its attackers and cause are unknown, and it should not be synchronized automatically with every coastal destruction.
timelineEvents.label: Kilise Tepe · destruction

timelineEvents.title: Ramesses III’s land battle in the Djahy frontier
timelineEvents.summary: Ramesses III describes land fighting and a naval victory at the river mouths. Combat, capture and subsequent settlement have different outcomes.
timelineEvents.details: Ramesses III records land fighting and a naval battle at the river mouths in his year 8. The usual c. 1177/1175 BCE date depends on Egyptian chronology; this map uses 1175. The exact battlefield locations, relationship and sequence of the scenes are debated. Both events share one display year; authored list order does not establish a historical sequence. Djahy is a broad Levantine frontier designation. The coordinate is a regional label anchor near the Egypt–southern Canaan approach, not a securely identified battlefield. Scholars disagree between a Levantine setting and northwest Sinai near the maritime encounter. Reliefs include carts, women and children; those depictions are not a complete army or migrant census. The main year 8 coalition lists Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen and Weshesh; Egyptian-service Sherden are not automatically included as hostile combatants.

timelineEvents.title: Philistia: new coastal communities
timelineEvents.summary: Aegean-connected newcomers and local communities participate in early Philistine society.
timelineEvents.details: Early Iron Age material culture and the Ashkelon genetic study support an incoming component followed by substantial local integration. Neither supplies an exact arrival year, a migrant census or proof that every coastal city was violently conquered. This display window follows the selected settlement chronology. Ancestry percentages are not copied into migrant totals.
timelineEvents.label: Philistia · coastal settlement

timelineEvents.title: Living captives settled in Egyptian strongholds
timelineEvents.dateLabel: After the year 8 campaign · early/mid12th centuryBCE
timelineEvents.summary: Papyrus Harris I describes Sherden and Weshesh captives brought to Egypt and settled in strongholds. They remain living residents.
timelineEvents.details: The reign-summary passage Harris I76.6–9 places Sherden and Weshesh immediately before capture and stronghold settlement. Its very large rhetorical quantities are not a reliable census. It does not name the strongholds or prove that all captives went to Fayum, nor does it establish every later Philistine settlement as an Egyptian deportation. The displayed1174–1155 interval and Lower Egyptian coordinate provide a reconstructed post-campaign context, not dated foundation evidence. Early Sherden already serving Egypt remain a separate component within the inclusive surviving settler envelope.

timelineEvents.title: Sherden landholding in Middle Egypt
timelineEvents.dateLabel: Ramesses V, year 4 · mid12th centuryBCE (shown c. 1142)
timelineEvents.summary: The Wilbour land register attests settled Sherden in Middle Egypt. This is later resident evidence, not a new migration or an all-Egypt census.
timelineEvents.details: The survey lists Sherden and Sherden-related military titles among landholders and cultivators; some entries concern children working a deceased holder’s land. It supports continuing communities and descendants, not identification of the same individual captives decades after battle. The supplied synthesis uses c. 1142 BCE; other chronologies date the document around 1147 BCE, so the regnal-year and period label take priority. The coordinate labels the broader Fayum/Middle Egyptian survey region and does not locate every recorded holding. Existing household conversions remain explicitly model assumptions inside the Egyptian settler envelope.

-1140.summary: Mycenae’s palace system ends amid destruction. The attackers, if any, are unidentified.
-1140.details: Several destruction episodes affected Mycenae, including earlier damage to buildings outside the citadel. The final palatial horizon belongs near the LH IIIB–IIIC transition. These episodes should not be combined into a single dated Sea Peoples conquest; neither the destruction deposits nor the later traditions identify a particular invading people.

-1140.title: Pylos: the palace burns

-1095.title: Mediterranean seafaring networks
-1095.summary: Traditional reconstructions connect western, Aegean and Anatolian seafarers through exchange, service and raids; their homelands remain disputed.

-1095.title: Perire: Merneptah defeats a Libyan-led coalition
-1095.summary: A Libyan-led coalition is defeated in the western Delta. Egyptian records distinguish enemy dead, living captives and the fleeing Libyan ruler.
-1095.details: Karnak names Meryey’s Libyan forces with Ekwesh, Teresh, Lukka, Sherden and Shekelesh. Its damaged account lists slain enemies and living prisoners separately. Hands and genital trophies are counting units for the dead, not extra people to add to the associated totals; the text specifically associates Ekwesh hand-taking with absence of foreskins. Athribis and Karnak preserve different or damaged figures. Familiar Medinet Habu piles of hands and phalli belong to Ramesses III’s year 5 Libyan victory, a later event. Perire’s coordinate is a western-Delta proxy. The existing 1,000/3,000/4,000 modeled deaths are separate visualization scenarios, not exact reconstructed source totals. Meryey’s flight supports rout; it does not document the destination of every allied survivor.

-1095.title: Hattusa: abandonment and burning

-1095.title: Sherden landholding in Middle Egypt
-1095.dateLabel: Ramesses V, year 4 · mid12th centuryBCE (shown c. 1142)
-1095.summary: The Wilbour land register attests settled Sherden in Middle Egypt. This is later resident evidence, not a new migration or an all-Egypt census.
-1095.details: The survey lists Sherden and Sherden-related military titles among landholders and cultivators; some entries concern children working a deceased holder’s land. It supports continuing communities and descendants, not identification of the same individual captives decades after battle. The supplied synthesis uses c. 1142 BCE; other chronologies date the document around 1147 BCE, so the regnal-year and period label take priority. The coordinate labels the broader Fayum/Middle Egyptian survey region and does not locate every recorded holding. Existing household conversions remain explicitly model assumptions inside the Egyptian settler envelope.

-1095.title: Philistia: new coastal communities
-1095.summary: Aegean-connected newcomers and local communities participate in early Philistine society.
-1095.details: Early Iron Age material culture and the Ashkelon genetic study support an incoming component followed by substantial local integration. Neither supplies an exact arrival year, a migrant census or proof that every coastal city was violently conquered. This display window follows the selected settlement chronology. Ancestry percentages are not copied into migrant totals.
